subject: Speed up a discontinuous time-series model

messages.author: 9860719641632b58
messages.subject: Speed up a discontinuous time-series model
parts:
Hello,

Inside my model function I do something like the following (this is strongly simplified, in order to stress my point.)
The model vector has a size (N) of a few hundred.

for (i in 1:N){

   if (time[i] > paramater1 ) {

      model[i] <- parameter2 );
      }

   else{ model[i] <- parameter3 ;
      }


This is obviously very slow and I wonder whether there is any way to speed it up.

time is ordered, positive and evenly spaced. Therefore the else statement will be executed until time[i] > parameter1
and from this point on only the if statement will be executed.

I am looking for away to avoid iterating the if else clause N times.

My first idea was to determine the index i, at which time[i] > parameter1 is True for the first time.
This should be given by sth like:

round ( parameter1 / ( time[2]-[time[1] ) )

This is does not work, since the ouput of Stan's rounding functions are real and can not be used as indices.


Would you see any other way around this? It makes my model almost intractably slow.

Thanks
Tammo

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Speed up a discontinuous time-series model
parts:
On Friday, August 29, 2014 11:52:15 PM UTC-4, Tammo Nikolas wrote:
Inside my model function I do something like the following (this is strongly simplified, in order to stress my point.)
The model vector has a size (N) of a few hundred.

for (i in 1:N){

   if (time[i] > paramater1 ) {

      model[i] <- parameter2 );
      }

   else{ model[i] <- parameter3 ;
      }


This is obviously very slow and I wonder whether there is any way to speed it up.

That is not obviously slow, and in a compiled language like C++, it would generally be obviously not slow. In the particular case of Stan, it may be slow for a not obvious reason: by having a discontinuity, the adaptation during the warmup can be thrown off and thus you might have a lot of unnecessarily small leapfrog steps.

I think you could eliminate the problem you stated with if and else using an initial while loop:

i <- 1;
while(time[i] > parameter1) {
  model[i] <- parameter2;
  i <- i + 1;
}
for(j in i:N) {
  model[j] <- parameter3;
}

but I would expect that to make no noticeable difference to the wall time.

Look at the metadata for the sampler (n_leapfrog__, n_divergent__, etc.) to see if the discontinuity is causing issues with the adaptation. If so, then hopefully there is some equivalent way to reformulate your model without the discontinuity.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Speed up a discontinuous time-series model
parts:
Each of those leapfrog steps is calculating the log probability
function and its gradient, which is where the time's going.

The reason you get so many steps is that Stan's had to crank down
the step size in order to hit your target acceptance probability.

That can either mean you have a really complicated posterior, but
it could also signal a bug in the model somewhere.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speed up a discontinuous time-series model
parts:
Firstly, 2047 is indicative of hitting the max_depth threshold in NUTS which will cause
large autocorrelations.  You should increase max_depth, but as Bob notes you’re only
hitting the threshold because the step size is so small.  This can very likely be due to
large curvature changes near the discontinuity.

The thing you have to realize with HMC is that the algorithm doesn’t suffer only when
the trajectory hits the discontinuity.  Every time the trajectory _passes_ the discontinuity
it should jump a bit, but we can’t simulate that and the resulting trajectories start to
drift from the true posterior.  Short answer — discontinuities are bad and, in particular,
all of our adaptation is not guaranteed to work any more.  Make your model smooth
by ensuring that the first derivatives match at the transition between the two regions.

Also, any continuous model with any n_divergent=1 iterations are bad.  You should
revisit those and decrease the step size until the divergent iterations go away.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speed up a discontinuous time-series model
parts:
The log probability function and its gradient should
be continuous.

Michael's talking about the problems you get when the gradients
are not continous. For instance,

fabs(x) = |x|

is continuous, but its derivative

d/dx fabs(x) = 1 if x > 0
-1 if x < 0
undefined if x = 0

is undefined at 0 and there's no way to fill in a value to
make it continuous.

- Bob
